newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Investors cheer Russia's moves to reform UES.
newsitem.headline: Investors cheer Russia's moves to reform UES.

text.p: Russia slammed the management of its largest company, the electricity utility UES, signalling on Tuesday that reform of the group was ready to begin.
Investors hailed the move by pushing up UES (Unified Energy System) shares although doubts remain over how the company can be restructured to create competition.
Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov said the government could increase control over the national power utility after blaming management for a non-payments crisis.
"Government control may be increased, as the company is a natural monopoly from the point of view of energy and transport," he told a news conference after a meeting devoted to restructuring UES.

UES is Russia's largest company by sales and employees and one of the huge, partially-regulated companies with no competitors -- like railways -- known as natural monopolies. The government owns 52 percent of it.

UES controls the national power grid, has controlling stakes in regional power utilities and has its own power plants. But Nemtsov said it owed the government 9.5 trillion roubles ($1.7 billion) and productivity had shrunk as the workforce increased.

Investors question how the company will be restructured to increase industry competition, but they pushed the share price of UES, the bellwether of the Russian Trading System, up 5.5 percent on Tuesday.

UES closed at $0.1995 after $0.1890 on Monday. It had been gradually falling since reaching a high of just under 26 cents at the end of February after a sharp rally at the the beginning of the year from under nine cents late last year.
Nemtsov said the company planned to reduce rates to manufacturing industry by 13 percent this year, which officials have said is crucial to improving industrial productivity.
Interfax news agency said the government had named special representatives including top reformers to UES and urged a long-term bond be prepared for issue this year.
"It is necessary to bring a consolidated government position to the company," said Nemtsov, appointed to Russia's new reformist cabinet to restructure natural monopolies.
He said UES closed-doors meetings to award contracts, some to foreigners, had to be stopped. Investor rights had to be respected and an independent auditor appointed.
Bill Browder, managing director of Hermitage Capital Management in Moscow, said the market was eager to understand government plans for UES, under development for weeks.
"There is so much confusion surrounding UES that any type of clarity will add to the share price. UES is a deeply undervalued company on all levels of valuation," he said.
Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow, said Nemtsov's plans were less than he had hoped for, but still positive.
"I thought this might be the occasion to unveil a genuine restructuring programme for the utility sector," he said.
"It seems like nothing has changed, except the atmosphere which has become more critical of Unified. That is good as far as it goes."

He said 1997 was likely to be a tough year for the power sector. Planned rate hikes for protected household consumers, who pay less than industrial consumers, would lag rate cuts for manufacturers, he estimated.
Utility collections, hampered by a countrywide payments crisis, would probably remain poor.
He said the UES share play was based on the timetable of reform. "Unified is going to be radically restructured -- it is just a question of when," he said.
